title: Pest identification and impact assessment processes

lessons.title: Identifying pests on the job
lessons.html:
Applying identification skills at work

In the workplace you will meet real pests in real conditions: half-crushed insects, old droppings mixed with fresh ones, frass of uncertain origin and clients who describe pests vaguely. This module develops your ability to identify pests reliably and assess their impact under supervision.

Building a personal reference collection

With your mentor's guidance, build a reference set of correctly identified specimens and photographs of common pests in your area: maize weevil, lesser grain borer, red flour beetle, Indian meal moth, German and American cockroaches, house fly, Norway rat, roof rat and house mouse droppings, termite mud tubes, borer exit holes and frass, and the main invader plants in your region. Label each with species, date and site type. Compare new finds with your collection.

Practical routine for each find

  1. Note the exact location and the conditions there: warm, damp, dusty, near food.
  2. Examine with a hand lens and photograph with a scale such as a ruler.
  3. Compare with your reference set and identification guides.
  4. Decide whether the evidence is fresh or old.
  5. If unsure, collect the specimen and ask your mentor or send it to a specialist.
  6. Record the identification and how it was confirmed.

Scenario

A feed mill manager complains of "small brown beetles" in bagged feed. You find reddish-brown beetles about 3 to 4 mm long in floury residues inside a conveyor, and very few in whole grain. With your mentor you confirm flour beetles, a secondary pest that thrives in fine residues. The cause points to poor cleaning of equipment rather than an infestation of incoming grain, which changes the recommendation from fumigating all stock to deep-cleaning the plant and targeted treatment.

lessons.title: Assessing impact and presenting findings
lessons.html:
Practising impact assessment

For each job, assess the infestation's extent and impact and present a recommendation. Your mentor will check your reasoning.

Questions to answer for each site

  • How widespread is the pest, and is activity increasing?
  • What is at risk: food safety, product value, structures, people, animals, export status or audit results?
  • How likely is harm, and how serious would it be?
  • What is causing or supporting the infestation?
  • What action is needed, by whom and how urgently?

Example risk ratings

FindingTypical rating
Mouse droppings in a food production roomHigh; immediate action
Live weevils in export maize due to load next weekHigh; urgent
Old borer holes with no fresh frass in a shedLow; monitor
Flies around a manure heap away from food areasModerate; sanitation and monitoring

Presenting to the client

Practise explaining your findings clearly: what the pest is, why it is there, what the risk is and what you recommend. Use evidence such as photographs and counts. Avoid exaggeration and avoid playing down serious risks.

Evidence for your portfolio

Keep identification records, specimen submission forms and replies, impact assessments and mentor feedback. Reflect on cases where your first identification was wrong and what you learned.

Key points

  • Build a labelled reference collection of local pests and their signs.
  • Follow a routine: location, hand lens, comparison, fresh or old, confirm if unsure.
  • Correct identification can change the whole recommendation, as with flour beetles in mill residues.
  • Rate risk by likelihood and severity and state urgency.
  • Present findings with evidence, without exaggeration, and keep records for your portfolio.
